expectedText:
SELF-HELP EVICTION AND LOCKOUT PROHIBITION (CIV. CODE § 789.3) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 · Pat Morgan

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's statutory prohibition on residential "self-help" eviction -- a landlord's use of utility shutoffs, lock changes, removal of doors or windows, or removal of a tenant's belongings to end an occupancy without a court process -- as it may apply to the residential property at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814, as between Pat Morgan and Jordan Lee. It states what California law provides under Civil Code § 789.3 and the related forcible-entry, Penal Code, and tenant-harassment provisions, and what California appellate courts have said about who those provisions protect, who can be liable, and how the statutory daily penalty is measured. It does not determine whether any specific act at 123 Main St., Apt. 4, Sacramento, CA 95814 violated any of these provisions, and it does not tell either Pat Morgan or Jordan Lee what to do about any specific dispute.

PROHIBITION ON WILLFUL INTERRUPTION OF UTILITY SERVICE TO END A RESIDENTIAL OCCUPANCY
Civil Code § 789.3(a) prohibits a landlord from willfully causing, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service furnished to a tenant, where the landlord acts with the intent to terminate the occupancy of property the tenant uses as a residence. The statute reaches an occupancy "under any lease or other tenancy or estate at will, however created," lists water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, elevator, and refrigeration as non-exclusive examples of covered utility services, and applies whether or not the utility service is under the landlord's control. The California Supreme Court, construing this subdivision, summarized its two operative requirements as willful interruption of a tenant's utility service coupled with the intent to terminate occupancy: a landlord violates the statute only when both are present.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "A landlord shall not with intent to terminate the occupancy under any lease or other tenancy or estate at will, however created, of property used by a tenant as his residence willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service furnished the tenant, including, but not limited to, water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, elevator, or refrigeration, whether or not the utility service is under the control of the landlord."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, prohibition on utility interruption with intent to terminate a residential occupancy (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "Thus a landlord violates the statute only when he willfully interrupts a tenant’s utility service with the intent to terminate occupancy."
  — Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348, California Supreme Court, the statute's two operative elements (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1270067/kinney-v-vaccari/)
  Known gap: Kinney v. Vaccari construed the version of § 789.3 in force before the 1979 amendment (Stats. 1979, Ch. 333), which the court quoted in full; the willfulness-plus-intent formulation quoted here tracks language in subdivision (a) that the amendment left in place, as confirmed by comparing the court's quotation of the former text against the current text fetched from the Legislature's site. The 1979 amendment added the lock-change, door/window, and personal-property prohibitions and restructured the penalty, changes addressed in the later clauses of this document. This clause does not address whether an interruption caused by nonpayment of a utility bill for reasons unrelated to any intent to terminate occupancy would satisfy the statute's intent element; the statute requires that intent, and the court in Kinney found it on the specific facts there.

PROHIBITION ON LOCKOUTS, REMOVAL OF DOORS OR WINDOWS, AND REMOVAL OF A TENANT'S BELONGINGS
In addition to the utility-interruption rule, Civil Code § 789.3(b) prohibits a landlord, acting with the same intent to terminate a residential occupancy, from willfully doing any of three things: preventing the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the property by changing the locks, using a bootlock, or using any other similar method or device; removing outside doors or windows; or removing the tenant's personal property, the furnishings, or any other items from the premises without the tenant's prior written consent, except when done under the separate statutory procedure for property left behind after a tenancy ends (Civil Code § 1980 and following). The subdivision states that nothing in it prevents the lawful eviction of a tenant by appropriate legal authorities, and that it does not apply to the transient-occupancy category described in Civil Code § 1940(b). A California Court of Appeal has described the lock-change prohibition in general terms: changing the locks on someone's dwelling without consent to force that person to leave is prohibited by statute.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "In addition, a landlord shall not, with intent to terminate the occupancy under any lease or other tenancy or estate at will, however created, of property used by a tenant as his or her residence, willfully:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(b) (chapeau) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the intent and willfulness requirements for the three additional prohibited acts (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "Prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the property by changing the locks or using a bootlock or by any other similar method or device;"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(b)(1) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, lock changes and similar devices (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "Remove outside doors or windows; or (3) Remove from the premises the tenant’s personal property, the furnishings, or any other items without the prior written consent of the tenant, except when done pursuant to the procedure set forth in Chapter 5 (commencing with Section 1980) of Title 5 of Part 4 of Division 3."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(b)(2)-(3) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, removal of outside doors or windows and removal of the tenant's personal property (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "Nothing in this subdivision shall be construed to prevent the lawful eviction of a tenant by appropriate legal authorities, nor shall anything in this subdivision apply to occupancies defined by subdivision (b) of Section 1940."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(b) (closing proviso) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, lawful evictions and transient occupancies excepted (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "First, as a general principle, changing the locks on someone’s dwelling without consent to force that person to leave is prohibited by statute."
  — Spinks v. Equity Residential Briarwood Apartments (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1004, California Court of Appeal, Sixth District, the lock-change prohibition stated as a general principle (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256783/spinks-v-equity-residential-briarwood-apartments/)
  Known gap: The exception for "occupancies defined by subdivision (b) of Section 1940" is stated by cross-reference; this document did not independently fetch § 1940(b), and relies on the Court of Appeal's description in Spinks that the excepted occupancies are those of transient hotel guests. The § 1980-et-seq. procedure for disposing of personal property left on the premises after a tenancy is addressed by a separate document in this corpus and is not described here. Spinks reversed a defense summary judgment and remanded; the sentence quoted from it is the court's statement of a general principle, not a finding that the defendants there violated § 789.3.

WHO THE STATUTE PROTECTS: RESIDENTIAL USE, NOT FULL-TIME OR PHYSICAL OCCUPANCY
Section 789.3 protects an occupancy of property "used by a tenant as his or her residence." California appellate decisions have read that phrase functionally. In Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park, the Court of Appeal held that a tenant need not live in the premises full-time to be a resident, reasoning that the statute's manifest purpose is to discourage landlords from using self-help and that limiting it to a permanent residence would defeat that purpose; the court also found no requirement that the tenant be in physical occupancy at the moment the utilities are shut off. In Spinks v. Equity Residential Briarwood Apartments, the Court of Appeal held that a person in peaceful possession of a residential dwelling need not be a "tenant" in the formal sense to be protected under § 789.3, applying the statute to a named occupant living in an apartment leased in her employer's name.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "We hold that a tenant need not live in the premises full-time in order to be a resident."
  — Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 1521, California Court of Appeal, Second District, holding that full-time residence is not required (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2275170/otanez-v-blue-skies-mobile-home-park/)
  "The manifest purpose of section 789.3 is to discourage landlords from using self-help. A construction of the statute that would limit its operation to property used as a permanent residence would defeat that purpose."
  — Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 1521, California Court of Appeal, the statute's purpose and the rejection of a permanent-residence limitation (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2275170/otanez-v-blue-skies-mobile-home-park/)
  "Nor is there any requirement in the statute that a tenant be in physical occupancy of the residence at the time the utilities are turned off."
  — Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 1521, California Court of Appeal, no physical-occupancy requirement at the time of the shutoff (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2275170/otanez-v-blue-skies-mobile-home-park/)
  "As explained above, however, a person in peaceful possession of a residential dwelling need not be a “tenant” to be protected under the relevant statutes."
  — Spinks v. Equity Residential Briarwood Apartments (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1004, California Court of Appeal, Sixth District, protection of a person in peaceful possession who is not formally a tenant (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256783/spinks-v-equity-residential-briarwood-apartments/)
  Known gap: Otanez held only that a reasonable trier of fact could find the tenant there used the mobilehome as a temporary or occasional residence; the court reversed a summary judgment rather than deciding residency as a matter of fact. Otanez also held, in the same opinion, that the statute does require that the property actually be used as a residence and not merely be rented for residential purposes -- a limitation this clause reports alongside the holding. Spinks likewise reversed a defense summary judgment; its statement that a person in peaceful possession need not be a "tenant" appears in the court's discussion of the plaintiff's statutory claims and rests in part on Civil Code § 1940(a), which this document did not independently fetch. In the CourtListener text of Spinks, the quoted sentence is interrupted by an official-reporter page-break marker ("*1049") between the words "relevant" and "statutes"; that marker is omitted from the quote as a non-textual artifact, and no other change was made.

WHO CAN BE LIABLE: THE LANDLORD, INCLUDING FOR A MANAGING AGENT'S ACTS
Section 789.3 imposes liability on a "landlord." Two California appellate decisions address how that term operates when the acts are carried out by someone else. In Otanez, the Court of Appeal held that the mobilehome park's managers -- who had no ownership interest in the park -- could not be held liable under § 789.3 in their own right, because the statute does not apply to persons other than landlords, and the agents' acts were wrongful only because the statute proscribed them. In Kinney v. Vaccari, by contrast, the California Supreme Court affirmed a judgment holding the property owner liable for the § 789.3 penalties arising from his son and managing agent's acts, on the basis that the acts were within the scope of the agent's employment under the doctrine of respondeat superior.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Here the acts of the managers were not wrongful in their nature. The acts are wrongful only if they are proscribed by statute. Because section 789.3 does not apply to persons other than landlords, we can see no basis for holding the managers liable."
  — Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 1521, California Court of Appeal, property managers not liable under the statute in their own right (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2275170/otanez-v-blue-skies-mobile-home-park/)
  "Although Senior was the actual landlord and Junior was his agent, the trial court held Senior liable for Junior’s acts within the scope of his employment under the doctrine of respondeat superior."
  — Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348, California Supreme Court, owner held liable for managing agent's acts under respondeat superior (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1270067/kinney-v-vaccari/)
  Known gap: These two decisions address different questions -- an agent's personal liability under the statute (Otanez) and an owner's vicarious liability for an agent's conduct (Kinney) -- and this clause does not treat either as resolving the other. The Kinney discussion quoted here appears in a footnote of the opinion, and the court also noted an alternative ratification finding by the trial court. Whether any particular person is a "landlord" for purposes of § 789.3 depends on facts this document does not evaluate.

CIVIL REMEDIES: ACTUAL DAMAGES, A DAILY STATUTORY AMOUNT, ATTORNEY'S FEES, AND INJUNCTIVE RELIEF
Civil Code § 789.3(c) makes a landlord who violates the section liable to the tenant in a civil action for the tenant's actual damages and for an additional amount of up to $100 for each day or part of a day the landlord remains in violation. In fixing that amount, the court considers proof of such matters as justice may require, but in no event may less than $250 be awarded for each separate cause of action; subsequent or repeated violations not committed contemporaneously with the initial violation are treated as separate causes of action subject to a separate award. Under subdivision (d), the court must award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party in any such action, the tenant may seek injunctive relief to prevent continuing or further violations while the action is pending, and the statutory remedy is not exclusive of any other remedy the tenant may have under other law. The attorney's-fee provision runs to whichever party prevails: in Spinks, the trial court had awarded the defendant landlord its fees under § 789.3 after granting summary judgment, an award the Court of Appeal vacated only because its reversal of the judgment meant there was no longer a prevailing party.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "(1) Actual damages of the tenant. (2) An amount not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100) for each day or part thereof the landlord remains in violation of this section. In determining the amount of such award, the court shall consider proof of such matters as justice may require; however, in no event shall less than two hundred fifty dollars ($250) be awarded for each separate cause of action. Subsequent or repeated violations, which are not committed contemporaneously with the initial violation, shall be treated as separate causes of action and shall be subject to a separate award of damages."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(c)(1)-(2) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, actual damages and the daily statutory amount with a $250 minimum per cause of action (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "In any action under subdivision (c) the court shall award reasonable attorney’s fees to the prevailing party. In any such action the tenant may seek appropriate injunctive relief to prevent continuing or further violation of the provisions of this section during the pendency of the action. The remedy provided by this section is not exclusive and shall not preclude the tenant from pursuing any other remedy which the tenant may have under any other provision of law."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 789.3(d) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, mandatory attorney's fees to the prevailing party, injunctive relief, and non-exclusivity (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=789.3.)
  "Where summary judgment is reversed on appeal, there is no prevailing party and thus no basis for an award of fees."
  — Spinks v. Equity Residential Briarwood Apartments (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1004, California Court of Appeal, Sixth District, a fee award to a defendant landlord under § 789.3 vacated for want of a prevailing party after reversal (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2256783/spinks-v-equity-residential-briarwood-apartments/)
  Known gap: The daily amount in subdivision (c)(2) is a ceiling ("not to exceed"), not a fixed figure; the pre-1980 version of the statute construed in Kinney v. Vaccari imposed a mandatory $100 per day, and the constitutional limits the Supreme Court discussed in that context are addressed in the next clause. Spinks did not decide whether or when a defendant landlord may recover fees under subdivision (d); the court expressly declined to address the reach of the fee provision because its reversal left no prevailing party. This clause does not quantify actual damages, which depend on facts not evaluated here.

HOW COURTS MEASURE THE DAILY AMOUNT: PER RENTAL UNIT, SUBJECT TO CONSTITUTIONAL LIMITS
The California Supreme Court has construed the word "tenant" in the penalty formula of § 789.3 to refer to all the occupants of a rental unit, so that the daily statutory amount is measured per unit rather than multiplied by the number of individual occupants; the court reasoned that multiplying a mandatory, fixed, and cumulative sanction by the number of occupants would often lead to unduly harsh results, and that the interests of multiple occupants are protected by their individual right to actual damages. The same court had earlier held, in Hale v. Morgan, that the daily penalty as then written could produce constitutionally excessive results in a given case; in Kinney it upheld a $36,000 penalty for a 60-day winter gas shutoff affecting six units as proportioned to the landlord's misconduct and not constitutionally excessive, emphasizing the landlord's lack of provocation, the tenants' repeated efforts to pay rent and restore service, and the hardship to the occupants, including minor children.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Thus, we agree with the trial court that “tenant” as used in the penalty formula of section 789.3 refers to all the occupants of a rental unit. The interests of multiple occupants of a single unit are adequately protected by their individual right to actual damages under the statute."
  — Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348, California Supreme Court, "tenant" in the penalty formula means all occupants of a rental unit (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1270067/kinney-v-vaccari/)
  "we declared that “section 789.3 permits the assessment of arbitrary, excessive and unreasonable penalties” and in certain situations the imposition of the $100 daily penalty can be “‘clearly, positively, and unmistakably’ unconstitutional. ” As will appear, the present action is not such a case."
  — Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348, California Supreme Court, describing Hale v. Morgan's constitutional limit on the penalty (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1270067/kinney-v-vaccari/)
  "Thus, we conclude that the punitive assessments imposed by the trial court here are “both proportioned to the landlord’s misconduct and necessary to achieve the penalty’s deterrent purposes”"
  — Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348, California Supreme Court, the penalty upheld on the facts (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1270067/kinney-v-vaccari/)
  "We also note that in its 1979 session the Legislature substantially rewrote section 789.3 in a number of respects. First, the revision added three further acts that landlords are prohibited from doing with the intent to evict, to wit, changing locks on the rented premises, removing its doors or windows, and removing the tenant’s personal property or furnishings."
  — Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348 (fn. 6), California Supreme Court, noting the 1979 rewrite of the statute (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/1270067/kinney-v-vaccari/)
  Known gap: Both Hale v. Morgan (1978) 22 Cal.3d 388 and Kinney construed the pre-1980 text of § 789.3, under which the $100 daily penalty was mandatory in amount; the Kinney court itself noted, in a footnote, that the Legislature substantially rewrote the section in 1979 to make the daily amount a ceiling, to direct courts to consider such matters as justice may require, and to set a $250 minimum per cause of action, and it expressly declined to determine the relevance of that change. Hale was not independently fetched for this document; its holding is reported here only as the Kinney opinion describes and quotes it. Whether the Hale proportionality analysis retains force under the amended, discretionary penalty is a question this document does not resolve.

RELATED LAW: FORCIBLE ENTRY AND THE PENAL CODE MISDEMEANOR
Separate from § 789.3, California's summary-proceedings statutes define "forcible entry." Under Code of Civil Procedure § 1159, a person is guilty of a forcible entry who either enters upon or into real property by breaking open doors, windows, or other parts of a house, or by any kind of violence or circumstance of terror, or who, after entering peaceably, turns out the party in possession by force, threats, or menacing conduct. The statute defines "party in possession" as any person who hires real property, including a boarder or lodger, but excluding the transient occupancies described in Civil Code § 1940(b). The Penal Code separately makes it a misdemeanor to use, or to procure, encourage, or assist another to use, any force or violence in entering upon or detaining lands or other possessions of another, except in the cases and in the manner allowed by law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "Every person is guilty of a forcible entry who either: (1) By breaking open doors, windows, or other parts of a house, or by any kind of violence or circumstance of terror enters upon or into any real property. (2) Who, after entering peaceably upon real property, turns out by force, threats, or menacing conduct, the party in possession."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1159(a) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, the two forms of forcible entry (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1159.)
  "For purposes of this section, “party in possession” means any person who hires real property and includes a boarder or lodger, except those persons whose occupancy is described in subdivision (b) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code."
  — Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1159(b) (California Legislative Information text), Code of Civil Procedure, definition of "party in possession" (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CCP&sectionNum=1159.)
  "Every person using or procuring, encouraging or assisting another to use, any force or violence in entering upon or detaining any lands or other possessions of another, except in the cases and in the manner allowed by law, is guilty of a misdemeanor."
  — Cal. Penal Code § 418 (California Legislative Information text), Penal Code, misdemeanor for forcible entry or detainer (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=PEN&sectionNum=418.)
  Known gap: This clause reports only the definitional section of the forcible entry and detainer chapter (Code Civ. Proc. §§ 1159-1179a); the procedural provisions and remedies in the rest of that chapter, including the forcible detainer definition in § 1160 and the damages provisions, were not fetched or quoted. Penal Code § 418 is a criminal statute enforced by public prosecutors; this document does not describe how or whether any prosecuting agency applies it to landlord-tenant lockouts. Neither statute uses the term "self-help," and this clause does not assert that every § 789.3 violation is also a forcible entry or a § 418 misdemeanor, or the reverse.

RELATED LAW: FORCE, THREATS, OR MENACING CONDUCT TO INFLUENCE A TENANT TO VACATE (CIV. CODE § 1940.2)
Civil Code § 1940.2 makes it unlawful for a landlord, for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling, to use or threaten to use force, willful threats, or menacing conduct constituting a course of conduct that interferes with the tenant's quiet enjoyment of the premises in violation of Civil Code § 1927 and that would create an apprehension of harm in a reasonable person; the statute states that a tenant need not be actually or constructively evicted to obtain relief under that paragraph. A tenant who prevails in a civil action, including a small claims action, to enforce rights under § 1940.2 is entitled to a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. The section also provides that a good-faith oral or written warning notice about conduct that violates or may violate the rental agreement, rules, or laws, and an explanation of those terms given in the normal course of business, are not violations.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-10]
  "It is unlawful for a landlord to do any of the following for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling:"
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(a) (chapeau) and (a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, force, willful threats, or menacing conduct to influence a tenant to vacate (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  "Use, or threaten to use, force, willful threats, or menacing conduct constituting a course of conduct that interferes with the tenant’s quiet enjoyment of the premises in violation of Section 1927 that would create an apprehension of harm in a reasonable person. Nothing in this paragraph requires a tenant to be actually or constructively evicted in order to obtain relief."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(a)(3) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, the force-or-menacing-conduct category and the no-eviction-required clause (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  "A tenant who prevails in a civil action, including an action in small claims court, to enforce his or her rights under this section is entitled to a civil penalty in an amount not to exceed two thousand dollars ($2,000) for each violation."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(b) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, civil penalty of up to $2,000 per violation (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  "An oral or written warning notice, given in good faith, regarding conduct by a tenant, occupant, or guest that violates, may violate, or violated the applicable rental agreement, rules, regulations, lease, or laws, is not a violation of this section. An oral or written explanation of the rental agreement, rules, regulations, lease, or laws given in the normal course of business is not a violation of this section."
  — Cal. Civ. Code § 1940.2(c) (California Legislative Information text), Civil Code, good-faith warnings and explanations are not violations (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=CIV&sectionNum=1940.2.)
  Known gap: Section 1940.2(a) lists five categories of unlawful conduct; this clause quotes only the force-or-menacing-conduct category in paragraph (3). The other four -- conduct violating Penal Code § 484(a) (theft) or § 518 (extortion), a significant and intentional violation of the entry statute (Civil Code § 1954), and threats to disclose immigration or citizenship status -- are not quoted here; the § 1954 category is addressed in this corpus's Landlord's Right of Entry information sheet. Penal Code §§ 484 and 518 and Civil Code § 1927 were not fetched for this document. Subdivision (d), which states that the section neither enlarges nor diminishes a landlord's right to terminate a tenancy under existing law or a local government's ability to regulate landlord harassment, is summarized from the fetched text but not quoted.

It does not constitute legal advice about, and does not resolve, any specific dispute concerning the property.

expectedJSON.body: Section 789.3 protects an occupancy of property "used by a tenant as his or her residence." California appellate decisions have read that phrase functionally. In Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park, the Court of Appeal held that a tenant need not live in the premises full-time to be a resident, reasoning that the statute's manifest purpose is to discourage landlords from using self-help and that limiting it to a permanent residence would defeat that purpose; the court also found no requirement that the tenant be in physical occupancy at the moment the utilities are shut off. In Spinks v. Equity Residential Briarwood Apartments, the Court of Appeal held that a person in peaceful possession of a residential dwelling need not be a "tenant" in the formal sense to be protected under § 789.3, applying the statute to a named occupant living in an apartment leased in her employer's name.

citations.quote: We hold that a tenant need not live in the premises full-time in order to be a resident.

citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, the statute's purpose and the rejection of a permanent-residence limitation
citations.quote: The manifest purpose of section 789.3 is to discourage landlords from using self-help. A construction of the statute that would limit its operation to property used as a permanent residence would defeat that purpose.

citations.case: Otanez v. Blue Skies Mobile Home Park (1991) 1 Cal.App.4th 1521
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, no physical-occupancy requirement at the time of the shutoff
citations.quote: Nor is there any requirement in the statute that a tenant be in physical occupancy of the residence at the time the utilities are turned off.

citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, Sixth District, protection of a person in peaceful possession who is not formally a tenant
citations.quote: As explained above, however, a person in peaceful possession of a residential dwelling need not be a “tenant” to be protected under the relevant statutes.

Otanez also held, in the same opinion, that the statute does require that the property actually be used as a residence and not merely be rented for residential purposes -- a limitation this clause reports alongside the holding. Spinks likewise reversed a defense summary judgment; its statement that a person in peaceful possession need not be a "tenant" appears in the court's discussion of the plaintiff's statutory claims and rests in part on Civil Code § 1940(a), which this document did not independently fetch. In the CourtListener text of Spinks, the quoted sentence is interrupted by an official-reporter page-break marker ("*1049") between the words "relevant" and "statutes"; that marker is omitted from the quote as a non-textual artifact, and no other change was made.

expectedJSON.body: Section 789.3 imposes liability on a "landlord." Two California appellate decisions address how that term operates when the acts are carried out by someone else. In Otanez, the Court of Appeal held that the mobilehome park's managers -- who had no ownership interest in the park -- could not be held liable under § 789.3 in their own right, because the statute does not apply to persons other than landlords, and the agents' acts were wrongful only because the statute proscribed them. In Kinney v. Vaccari, by contrast, the California Supreme Court affirmed a judgment holding the property owner liable for the § 789.3 penalties arising from his son and managing agent's acts, on the basis that the acts were within the scope of the agent's employment under the doctrine of respondeat superior.

citations.quote: Here the acts of the managers were not wrongful in their nature. The acts are wrongful only if they are proscribed by statute. Because section 789.3 does not apply to persons other than landlords, we can see no basis for holding the managers liable.

citations.case: Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, owner held liable for managing agent's acts under respondeat superior
citations.quote: Although Senior was the actual landlord and Junior was his agent, the trial court held Senior liable for Junior’s acts within the scope of his employment under the doctrine of respondeat superior.

The Kinney discussion quoted here appears in a footnote of the opinion, and the court also noted an alternative ratification finding by the trial court. Whether any particular person is a "landlord" for purposes of § 789.3 depends on facts this document does not evaluate.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 789.3(c) makes a landlord who violates the section liable to the tenant in a civil action for the tenant's actual damages and for an additional amount of up to $100 for each day or part of a day the landlord remains in violation. In fixing that amount, the court considers proof of such matters as justice may require, but in no event may less than $250 be awarded for each separate cause of action; subsequent or repeated violations not committed contemporaneously with the initial violation are treated as separate causes of action subject to a separate award. Under subdivision (d), the court must award reasonable attorney's fees to the prevailing party in any such action, the tenant may seek injunctive relief to prevent continuing or further violations while the action is pending, and the statutory remedy is not exclusive of any other remedy the tenant may have under other law. The attorney's-fee provision runs to whichever party prevails: in Spinks, the trial court had awarded the defendant landlord its fees under § 789.3 after granting summary judgment, an award the Court of Appeal vacated only because its reversal of the judgment meant there was no longer a prevailing party.

citations.quote: (1) Actual damages of the tenant. (2) An amount not to exceed one hundred dollars ($100) for each day or part thereof the landlord remains in violation of this section. In determining the amount of such award, the court shall consider proof of such matters as justice may require; however, in no event shall less than two hundred fifty dollars ($250) be awarded for each separate cause of action. Subsequent or repeated violations, which are not committed contemporaneously with the initial violation, shall be treated as separate causes of action and shall be subject to a separate award of damages.

citations.quote: In any action under subdivision (c) the court shall award reasonable attorney’s fees to the prevailing party. In any such action the tenant may seek appropriate injunctive relief to prevent continuing or further violation of the provisions of this section during the pendency of the action. The remedy provided by this section is not exclusive and shall not preclude the tenant from pursuing any other remedy which the tenant may have under any other provision of law.

citations.case: Spinks v. Equity Residential Briarwood Apartments (2009) 171 Cal.App.4th 1004
citations.cite: California Court of Appeal, Sixth District, a fee award to a defendant landlord under § 789.3 vacated for want of a prevailing party after reversal
citations.quote: Where summary judgment is reversed on appeal, there is no prevailing party and thus no basis for an award of fees.

Vaccari imposed a mandatory $100 per day, and the constitutional limits the Supreme Court discussed in that context are addressed in the next clause. Spinks did not decide whether or when a defendant landlord may recover fees under subdivision (d); the court expressly declined to address the reach of the fee provision because its reversal left no prevailing party. This clause does not quantify actual damages, which depend on facts not evaluated here.

expectedJSON.body: The California Supreme Court has construed the word "tenant" in the penalty formula of § 789.3 to refer to all the occupants of a rental unit, so that the daily statutory amount is measured per unit rather than multiplied by the number of individual occupants; the court reasoned that multiplying a mandatory, fixed, and cumulative sanction by the number of occupants would often lead to unduly harsh results, and that the interests of multiple occupants are protected by their individual right to actual damages. The same court had earlier held, in Hale v. Morgan, that the daily penalty as then written could produce constitutionally excessive results in a given case; in Kinney it upheld a $36,000 penalty for a 60-day winter gas shutoff affecting six units as proportioned to the landlord's misconduct and not constitutionally excessive, emphasizing the landlord's lack of provocation, the tenants' repeated efforts to pay rent and restore service, and the hardship to the occupants, including minor children.

citations.quote: Thus, we agree with the trial court that “tenant” as used in the penalty formula of section 789.3 refers to all the occupants of a rental unit. The interests of multiple occupants of a single unit are adequately protected by their individual right to actual damages under the statute.

citations.case: Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348
citations.cite: California Supreme Court, describing Hale v. Morgan's constitutional limit on the penalty
citations.quote: we declared that “section 789.3 permits the assessment of arbitrary, excessive and unreasonable penalties” and in certain situations the imposition of the $100 daily penalty can be “‘clearly, positively, and unmistakably’ unconstitutional. ” As will appear, the present action is not such a case.

citations.quote: Thus, we conclude that the punitive assessments imposed by the trial court here are “both proportioned to the landlord’s misconduct and necessary to achieve the penalty’s deterrent purposes”

citations.case: Kinney v. Vaccari (1980) 27 Cal.3d 348 (fn. 6)

citations.quote: We also note that in its 1979 session the Legislature substantially rewrote section 789.3 in a number of respects. First, the revision added three further acts that landlords are prohibited from doing with the intent to evict, to wit, changing locks on the rented premises, removing its doors or windows, and removing the tenant’s personal property or furnishings.

Morgan (1978) 22 Cal.3d 388 and Kinney construed the pre-1980 text of § 789.3, under which the $100 daily penalty was mandatory in amount; the Kinney court itself noted, in a footnote, that the Legislature substantially rewrote the section in 1979 to make the daily amount a ceiling, to direct courts to consider such matters as justice may require, and to set a $250 minimum per cause of action, and it expressly declined to determine the relevance of that change. Hale was not independently fetched for this document; its holding is reported here only as the Kinney opinion describes and quotes it. Whether the Hale proportionality analysis retains force under the amended, discretionary penalty is a question this document does not resolve.

expectedJSON.body: Separate from § 789.3, California's summary-proceedings statutes define "forcible entry." Under Code of Civil Procedure § 1159, a person is guilty of a forcible entry who either enters upon or into real property by breaking open doors, windows, or other parts of a house, or by any kind of violence or circumstance of terror, or who, after entering peaceably, turns out the party in possession by force, threats, or menacing conduct. The statute defines "party in possession" as any person who hires real property, including a boarder or lodger, but excluding the transient occupancies described in Civil Code § 1940(b). The Penal Code separately makes it a misdemeanor to use, or to procure, encourage, or assist another to use, any force or violence in entering upon or detaining lands or other possessions of another, except in the cases and in the manner allowed by law.

citations.quote: Every person is guilty of a forcible entry who either: (1) By breaking open doors, windows, or other parts of a house, or by any kind of violence or circumstance of terror enters upon or into any real property. (2) Who, after entering peaceably upon real property, turns out by force, threats, or menacing conduct, the party in possession.

citations.case: Cal. Code Civ. Proc. § 1159(b) (California Legislative Information text)
citations.cite: Code of Civil Procedure, definition of "party in possession"
citations.quote: For purposes of this section, “party in possession” means any person who hires real property and includes a boarder or lodger, except those persons whose occupancy is described in subdivision (b) of Section 1940 of the Civil Code.

citations.cite: Penal Code, misdemeanor for forcible entry or detainer
citations.quote: Every person using or procuring, encouraging or assisting another to use, any force or violence in entering upon or detaining any lands or other possessions of another, except in the cases and in the manner allowed by law, is guilty of a misdemeanor.

Proc. §§ 1159-1179a); the procedural provisions and remedies in the rest of that chapter, including the forcible detainer definition in § 1160 and the damages provisions, were not fetched or quoted. Penal Code § 418 is a criminal statute enforced by public prosecutors; this document does not describe how or whether any prosecuting agency applies it to landlord-tenant lockouts. Neither statute uses the term "self-help," and this clause does not assert that every § 789.3 violation is also a forcible entry or a § 418 misdemeanor, or the reverse.

expectedJSON.body: Civil Code § 1940.2 makes it unlawful for a landlord, for the purpose of influencing a tenant to vacate a dwelling, to use or threaten to use force, willful threats, or menacing conduct constituting a course of conduct that interferes with the tenant's quiet enjoyment of the premises in violation of Civil Code § 1927 and that would create an apprehension of harm in a reasonable person; the statute states that a tenant need not be actually or constructively evicted to obtain relief under that paragraph. A tenant who prevails in a civil action, including a small claims action, to enforce rights under § 1940.2 is entitled to a civil penalty of up to $2,000 for each violation. The section also provides that a good-faith oral or written warning notice about conduct that violates or may violate the rental agreement, rules, or laws, and an explanation of those terms given in the normal course of business, are not violations.
